text: Attacker-controlled JSON numbers reach unguarded BigDecimal conversions in JsonNumberImpl, bypassing the bigIntegerScaleLimit defense. The public accessors intValue() (line 262, sink 264), intValueExact() (267, sink 269), longValue() (272, sink 274), longValueExact() (277, sink 279) and doubleValue() (282, sink 284) all call bigDecimalValue().<conv>() with NO scale check, while the immediately following siblings bigIntegerValue() (287) and bigIntegerValueExact() (297) DO guard with `Math.abs(bd.scale()) <= bigIntegerScaleLimit` and otherwise throw UnsupportedOperationException(NUMBER_SCALE_LIMIT_EXCEPTION). The other number defense does not cover this: JsonTokenizer.getBigDecimal only limits the *source character count* (`sourceLen > jsonContext.bigDecimalLengthLimit()`, line 522, DEFAULT_MAX_BIGDECIMAL_LEN=1100), so a 13-character JSON literal such as {"a":1E+2147483647} passes the length check and yields a BigDecimal with scale -2147483647, which then flows unguarded into intValueExact()/longValueExact(). Source: JsonValueBodyReader.readFrom (rest/.../JsonValueBodyReader.java:69-70, reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1) parses an untrusted HTTP entity with Json.createReaderFactory(null) (defaults), and JsonParserImpl:171 builds the number via getJsonNumber(getBigDecimal(), jsonContext.bigIntegerScaleLimit()). This is the same incomplete-fix shape as the original scale-limit hardening: the limit was applied to the BigInteger accessors only. A verifier must confirm the JDK BigDecimal behaviour (intValueExact/longValueExact perform setScale(0)/toBigInteger, materializing a ~2^31-digit unscaled value) to establish the CPU/memory exhaustion.

text: MISSING max-string/token-length limit in the tokenizer. org.eclipse.parsson.JsonTokenizer.fillBuf() grows its character buffer by unconditional doubling (`char[] doubleBuf = Arrays.copyOf(buf, 2 * buf.length)`) whenever a single JSON token does not fit the current buffer (guard is only `storeLen == buf.length`). There is NO upper bound on the resulting array size and no corresponding configuration knob anywhere in the library: JsonContext's complete control surface is exactly bigIntegerScaleLimit(), bigDecimalLengthLimit(), depthLimit(), prettyPrinting(), rejectDuplicateKeys(), bufferPool() -- there is no maxStringLength/maxNameLength/maxDocumentSize. A single unterminated or very long string/name/number token in attacker-supplied JSON therefore forces repeated doubling until OutOfMemoryError (CWE-770 / CWE-789 uncontrolled resource allocation). Aggravating detail: line 479 recycles the OLD small buffer into the shared BufferPool while the newly doubled buffer replaces it, so oversized buffers can later pollute the pool. fillBuf is attacker-reachable (reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=8).

text: The JAX-RS entity reader hardcodes an un-hardenable parser configuration. org.eclipse.parsson.media.JsonValueBodyReader initializes its factory as `Json.createReaderFactory(null)` (line 45) -- a hardcoded null config map -- and then parses the entire untrusted HTTP request entity with `rf.createReader(inputStream).readValue()` (lines 69-70). Because the config map is null, none of Parsson's hardening knobs (JsonConfig.MAX_DEPTH, MAX_BIGINTEGER_SCALE, MAX_BIGDECIMAL_LEN, REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS) can be set per-application for this reader; a deployer can only influence them via JVM-wide system properties. Unlike its sibling JsonValueBodyWriter -- which does build a props map and call createWriterFactory(props) (lines 69-73) -- the reader offers no configuration path at all, and the reader is the side that handles attacker-controlled bytes. There is also no request-entity size cap, which is what makes the unbounded JsonTokenizer.fillBuf doubling (lead 1) remotely driveable for any app registering this provider (CWE-1188 insecure default / CWE-770).

text: MISSING nonce randomness in OAuth 1.0a request signing. org.eclipse.parsson.demos.twitter.TwitterObjectSearch builds its OAuth signature base-string parameter map with a hardcoded constant nonce: `put("oauth_nonce", "4b25256957d75b6370f33a4501dc5e7e")`, carrying an explicit `// TODO` comment in the source, alongside `put("oauth_signature_method", "HMAC-SHA1")` and `put("oauth_timestamp", "" + timestamp)`. OAuth 1.0a requires a per-request unique nonce; the anti-replay control is simply absent (no SecureRandom/UUID generation appears in the map initializer). Every signed request reuses the same nonce value, defeating server-side replay detection for the nonce+timestamp pair (CWE-323 reusing a nonce in a cryptographic protocol / CWE-330 insufficiently random values). Scope caveat for the verifier: this is demo/sample code under demos/twitter, not the shipped impl/ library, so real-world impact is limited to anyone copying the sample.

text: Json.createParserFactory(config) builds its JsonContext with a property whitelist of ONLY JsonContext.PROPERTY_BUFFER_POOL, omitting jakarta.json.JsonConfig.KEY_STRATEGY — while the sibling createReaderFactory (line 119) and createBuilderFactory (line 225) paths DO whitelist JsonConfig.REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS and KEY_STRATEGY. Because JsonContext.config(String) reads from that whitelist-filtered map (`return config != null ? config.get(propertyName) : null`), a KEY_STRATEGY the caller supplied is silently discarded on the parser-factory path. JsonParserImpl.getObject()/getValue() builds objects via `new JsonObjectBuilderImpl(jsonContext)` (JsonParserImpl.java:152 and :161), and JsonObjectBuilderImpl.java:53-54 resolves the duplicate-key policy as DuplicateStrategy.strategyFromProperty(jsonContext.config(KEY_STRATEGY), jsonContext.rejectDuplicateKeys()). With KEY_STRATEGY dropped to null and REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS unset, strategyFromProperty returns DuplicateStrategy.LAST, so duplicate object keys are silently accepted last-wins instead of being rejected. Net effect: the same config map that enforces duplicate-key rejection through Json.createReaderFactory(...) is a no-op through Json.createParserFactory(...) — a protection wired into two of three factory paths and omitted in the third, which is exactly the parser-disagreement primitive behind JSON duplicate-key auth-bypass / request-smuggling bugs.

text: JsonContext.copyPropertiesMap contains a switch whose `case JsonConfig.REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS:` branch is MISSING a `break;` — it conditionally puts the hardened value (`if (instance.rejectDuplicateKeys) newConfig.put(JsonConfig.REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS, true)` at line 235) and then falls straight through into `default:` at line 240 (`if (config.containsKey(propertyName)) newConfig.put(propertyName, config.get(propertyName))`), which re-puts the SAME key with the caller's raw value and overwrites the just-written `true`. The immediately preceding `case JsonGenerator.PRETTY_PRINTING:` branch does have its `break;`, so the omission is an asymmetry, and the comment "// Rest of properties are copied without changes" sits exactly where the `break;` should be — i.e. the deliberate protection-normalization step is silently undone by the fall-through. Concretely, a caller passing Map.of(JsonConfig.REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS, Boolean.FALSE) gets instance.rejectDuplicateKeys == true (because getBooleanProperty is presence-based: `config.containsKey(propertyName) ? true : null`) yet getConfigInUse() reports REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS=false, so the factory misreports its own duplicate-key protection state. Note for the verifier: the enforcement path JsonObjectBuilderImpl.java:53 reads the `rejectDuplicateKeys` FIELD rather than this map, so the direct impact appears confined to getConfigInUse() misreporting rather than outright protection loss — rank accordingly.

text: JsonObjectBuilderImpl.DuplicateStrategy.strategyFromProperty fails OPEN on an unrecognized KEY_STRATEGY value. The body is `if (value != null) { for (DuplicateStrategy s : values()) if (s.property.equals(value)) return s; } if (rejectDuplicateKeys) return NONE; else return LAST;` — when `value` is non-null but matches no strategy (most realistically when the application supplies a String such as "NONE" instead of the jakarta.json.JsonConfig.KeyStrategy enum constant, since `s.property` is a KeyStrategy and String.equals(enum) is always false), the loop silently falls out and, with REJECT_DUPLICATE_KEYS unset, the method returns DuplicateStrategy.LAST — duplicate keys are silently accepted last-wins. No exception is raised and nothing is logged, so an operator who believes they configured strict duplicate-key rejection gets none. This is a deliberate-looking asymmetry against the sibling config path in the same codebase: JsonContext.getIntProperty explicitly validates and THROWS `new JsonException(String.format("Could not convert %s property of type %s to Integer", ...))` on an unconvertible type, whereas the key-strategy path discards a bad value without complaint. The node is a chokepoint for attacker-reachable paths (centrality 4.85e-5, the highest observed in this scan), so the blast radius covers every object built through any builder or parser.

text: Inconsistent application of the bigIntegerScaleLimit guard across JsonNumberImpl accessors. The scale check `Math.abs(bd.scale()) <= bigIntegerScaleLimit` is applied ONLY in bigIntegerValue() (lines 290-291) and bigIntegerValueExact() (lines 300-301). The sibling accessors on the same class that also materialize the BigDecimal are NOT guarded: isIntegral() calls `bigDecimalValue().scale()` at line 259 and intValueExact() calls `bigDecimalValue().intValueExact()` at line 269, and per the semantic-search body text intValue()/longValue()/longValueExact()/doubleValue() are likewise unguarded. If any of those JDK BigDecimal accessors internally expands a hostile extreme-scale value (e.g. a parsed `1E-2147483647`) the scale cap is bypassed on that path. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for the verifier: whether this is actually exploitable depends on JDK BigDecimal internals (several of these have fast-paths that return 0 without expansion) AND on whether bigDecimalLengthLimit (default 1100) already rejects such a literal at parse time in JsonTokenizer -- I could not resolve either from the graph alone. Treat as a guard-asymmetry observation to confirm, not an established DoS.
